content: The laboratory network in the Western Pacific Region includes 383 laboratories, comprising one global specialized laboratory, three regional reference laboratories (RRLs), 17 national measles laboratories (NMLs), and, in China, 31 provincial and approximately 331 prefectural laboratories. In 2012, this network tested specimens from 18,528 suspected measles and rubella cases. The WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific accredits the RRLs, NMLs, and the 31 Chinese provincial laboratories, with nearly all network laboratories accredited as of March 2012. These laboratories are critical for serologic testing (ELISA) for anti-measles and anti-rubella IgM, as well as for genetic characterization of viruses detected from cases and outbreaks. The verification of measles elimination must be independently assessed for individual countries and areas, and eventually for the entire region, following standardized processes and criteria. For countries with large populations, such as China, verification may be conducted at a second-level administrative unit, but the Regional Verification Commission (RVC) will determine whether the country as a whole has achieved elimination. National Verification Committees (NVCs) will be established to collect, analyze, and validate national data, and to prepare and submit documentation to the RVC annually. National secretariats may assist NVCs in data collection and documentation preparation. Measles elimination requires the interruption of endemic measles virus transmission for at least 36 months to ensure sustainability. Documentation must address three criteria: evidence of interruption of endemic transmission for at least 36 months, verification-standard surveillance, and genotyping evidence supporting the interruption of endemic transmission. Surveillance must be sensitive enough to detect endemic cases and imported/import-related transmission chains, with adequate capacity for timely case investigation and laboratory analysis. Indicators for surveillance performance include: a national reporting rate of at least two non-measles, non-rubella cases per 100,000 population annually; adequate investigation of at least 80% of suspected cases; and adequate specimen collection from at least 80% of suspected cases. Laboratory performance indicators include: 100% accreditation of measles network laboratories by WHO, timely reporting of serologic results within four days of specimen receipt, and completion of virus detection and genotyping results within two months for at least 80% of specimens. Population immunity should be measured and presented by birth cohort, with additional evidence for marginalized and underserved groups. High levels of population immunity in every district are essential to interrupt endemic transmission and prevent re-establishment following virus importation. Experience in countries like Vietnam and the Philippines suggests that high coverage among children and adolescents is critical for sustaining elimination, even if adult immunity is not universally high.
